Four connected commercial functions. One operating point of view.

The Same Build in Four Industries

The Build OrderPart 10

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 14-minute read · Revenue

In short: We ran The Build Order through four composite firms in different sectors: a mid-market lender, a regional publisher, an industrial parts distributor and a luxury jeweller. The commercial line was the right place to start in all four, the wiring was necessary but not sufficient, and the best first agent was always unglamorous. The wider evidence points the same way. Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketers found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for AI, a reminder that every one of these firms started with a store that needed work before any agent could rely on it. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, which is why the first agents in all four firms targeted preparation and administration rather than the conversation itself. And Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027, on cost, unclear value or weak risk controls, describes exactly what a boring first agent and a logged gate are designed to avoid.

Two things changed with the sector. Regulation moved the decision record ahead of the first agent at the lender, and the time it takes for an outcome to arrive decided how fast each firm learned.

Key points

  • The order held in three of four firms and bent at the lender, where the record came before any agent.
  • Every sector has context that must never be connected: credit files, the newsroom, client confidences, unverified prices.
  • The shorter the outcome lag, the sooner the record pays: days for quotes, a season for clienteling, months for lending.
  • Review fatigue, brand safety, uncomfortable numbers and the human relationship were the four gateways that bit.
  • Three findings held everywhere: start commercial, wiring is not enough, and the first agent should be boring.

The first nine parts of this series set out a sequence for building a company's brain: three decisions before any tool, the commercial line as the starting point, the wiring, the record, a first agent and an approval gate. The obvious question is whether the sequence travels. Advisory and services firms have unusually clean commercial decisions: pitches are discrete, the people who win work also deliver it, and the CRM maps reasonably well to how the business runs.

This piece tests the sequence in four other sectors. Each firm is a composite, built from patterns across briefs and engagements rather than from any single company, and each section follows the same structure: where the commercial line really sits, what the wiring connects, the first record and first agent, the gateway that bit, and whether the order held.

A mid-market lender

Where the commercial line is. A lender of around 300 people grows through relationship managers and a network of brokers who refer business. Its commercial decisions are which referrals to prioritise, which pricing exceptions to approve and which brokers deserve more attention. All are frequent and similar, and their outcomes show within months: a loan funds or it does not.

The wiring. Email, calendar and the CRM connect as they would anywhere. The difference is what stays out. Identity checks, credit files and account data sit in systems the commercial build must not touch, and the data-access approver named at Gateway 0 does real work. A compliance officer, not the build owner, decides what crosses the wall.

The record and the first agent. Here the order bends. Before any agent drafts anything, the lender builds a record of pricing exceptions: the request, the reason, the approver, the expected outcome and the check date. In Regulators want the chain, not the model we argued that supervisors inspect the chain of evidence, approval and outcome rather than the model's internals, and supervisory commentary on autonomous AI in US broker-dealers points the same way. The first agent, when it arrives, prepares relationship managers for broker meetings from the CRM and that record. It writes nothing outbound.

The gateway that bit. Gateway 1. Every client-facing word already passes compliance review, so "nothing sends without a person" is an existing rule the system must respect. The friction is volume: once drafting is cheap, review queues fill. Our earlier piece Approval rate measures fatigue too is the warning: a reviewer approving almost every draft may simply be tired.

Did the order hold? No. The record moved ahead of the first agent, and the audit trail became part of the context layer rather than an addition to it.

A regional publisher

Where the commercial line is. A publisher of around 150 people across several titles earns most of its revenue from advertising and sponsorship. Its commercial decisions are which advertisers to pursue, when to grant a rate exception, and how to handle under-delivery through make-goods, credits and renewals.

The wiring. Rate cards, the inventory system and campaign delivery reports join the usual email, calendar and CRM. One wall matters more than any other: sales context must not reach the newsroom. An assistant that can see an advertiser's renewal thread and an editor's draft side by side breaches the publication's independence, whatever the permissions technically allow. The wiring is split by design into two context layers that never meet.

The record and the first agent. Rate exceptions become the first record, because they are frequent, similar and graded at renewal. The first agent chases insertion orders, compares delivery with what was sold, and drafts renewal briefs from the numbers. In builds like this the renewal brief is often the first AI output sales staff trust, because it is built from delivery data they can check.

The gateway that bit. Gateway 1, for a different reason: brand safety. A drafted message that misstates audience figures is a commercial problem; one that implies editorial influence is a reputational one. Approval rules are stricter for anything touching sponsored content.

Did the order hold? Yes: commercial first, then wiring, record and agent. It needed a firewall in the middle.

A parts distributor

Where the commercial line is. A distributor of around 220 people sells industrial components to manufacturers and contractors. Its commercial line is not a pipeline in the CRM sense; it is quoting. Inside sales staff answer requests for quotes all day, deciding which to quote, what discount to offer against the price book and what lead time to promise.

The wiring. The "CRM" turns out to be the ERP's customer table, plus the price book and a library of specification sheets. That changes the build more than the order. The context layer is mostly the ERP, and the definitions that matter are product codes, customer tiers and what counts as "in stock".

The record and the first agent. Quoting is close to the ideal case in Where judgment arrives first: thousands of similar decisions a year, outcomes known within days, and a sales director who defends margin every month. The record is the quote itself with two added fields: the reason for any discount beyond the standard tier, and the outcome. The first agent drafts quotes from the request, the price book and the customer's history, and places them in a queue for a person to check.

The gateway that bit. Gateway 2, the dollar figure. Because quotes are so measurable, the distributor reaches outcome write-back faster than the others, and the numbers are uncomfortable. Discounts the team believed were winning business turn out, once recorded, to win no more often than standard quotes in some product lines. That is the brain doing its job. It is also the moment the build stops being an IT project and becomes a pricing conversation.

Did the order hold? Yes, and it moved fastest. The lesson for other sectors is that the shorter the outcome lag, the sooner the record pays.

A luxury jeweller

Where the commercial line is. A jeweller of around 60 people, with showrooms and a wholesale arm, sells through client advisers and a network of dealers. Its commercial decisions are which clients to invite to private previews, which pieces to place with which dealers, and how to price bespoke commissions.

The wiring. The relationship lives in places most build plans ignore: advisers' client books, messaging apps and the order history in the commerce platform. Connecting them raises the sharpest consent question of the four. Clients shared anniversaries, preferences and sizes with an adviser, not with a system. The wiring follows what clients agreed to, and some of the most valuable context is deliberately never connected.

The record and the first agent. The first record is preview invitations: who was invited, why, and whether they bought within ninety days. Volume is lower than quoting but the decisions are similar enough to learn from across a season. The first agent prompts advisers rather than clients: an anniversary approaching, a piece matching a past request arriving, a dealer who has not reordered. The adviser decides whether to reach out.

The gateway that bit. Gateway 1, in reverse. The risk is not that a bad message is sent; it is that a good relationship starts to feel automated. The firm adopts a stricter rule than "nothing sends without a person": nothing reaches a client that the adviser did not write.

Did the order hold? Yes. The commercial line came first and the record paid back within a season, but the wiring step was smaller than anywhere else, by choice.

Three findings held in all four firms.

The commercial line was the right place to start. In every case it had the most frequent, most gradable decisions and someone who had to defend them.

The wiring was necessary and insufficient. Every firm got faster preparation from connecting its sources. None got a reason it had not recorded.

The best first agent was unglamorous. Meeting preparation, renewal briefs, draft quotes and reminders. Nothing autonomous reached a customer.

The wider evidence points the same way. Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketers found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for AI, a reminder that every one of these firms started with a store that needed work before any agent could rely on it. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, which is why the first agents in all four firms targeted preparation and administration rather than the conversation itself. And Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027, on cost, unclear value or weak risk controls, describes exactly what a boring first agent and a logged gate are designed to avoid.

Two things changed with the sector. Regulation moved the record ahead of the first agent at the lender. And the outcome lag set the pace of learning: days at the distributor, a season at the jeweller, months at the lender.

The shorter the time between a decision and its outcome, the sooner the record pays for itself.

Illustrative example: the distributor's discount rule
Decision
Stop discretionary discounts beyond the standard tier on two product lines for one quarter.
Reason and owner
Six months of recorded outcomes showed no higher win rate for discounted quotes in those lines. Owned by the sales director.
What changed
Quotes in those lines carry a flag so outcomes can be compared; the rule is reviewed after a quarter.

Illustrative: all four firms in this piece are composites built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • The commercial line travels. It looks different in every sector, but it is always where decisions are most frequent and most gradable.
  • Find the sector's wall. Credit files, the newsroom, client confidences: every industry has context that must never be connected.
  • Outcome lag sets the pace. The shorter it is, the sooner the record pays back.
  • Regulation moves the record forward. Where a supervisor will ask why, record before you automate.
Gateway card

Before moving to Gateway 2 in your sector

  • One commercial decision class recorded with reasons and outcomes
  • The sector's wall named and enforced in the wiring
  • A first agent that drafts but never sends
  • The outcome lag for your main decision measured

Common questions

Does the same AI build order work in every industry?

It held in three of the four sectors we tested. In regulated sectors such as lending, the decision record and audit trail should come before the first agent, because supervisors may ask the firm to reconstruct automated decisions.

What is the best first AI agent for a distributor?

A quoting assistant that drafts quotes from the price book and customer history into a review queue. Quotes are graded within days, so the record of discount reasons pays back quickly.

How should publishers use AI agents in ad sales?

For insertion orders, delivery reconciliation and renewal briefs, with a strict separation between sales and editorial context.

Can luxury retailers use AI without losing the personal touch?

Yes, if agents prompt client advisers rather than clients, and nothing reaches a client that the adviser did not write.
